newsitem.title: UK: BoE - stg strength to cut short-term inflation.
newsitem.headline: BoE - stg strength to cut short-term inflation.

text.p: Sterling's steep climb over the past seven months will lead to a fall in British inflation in the short run as import prices are depressed, the Bank of England said on Wednesday.
But that did not stop the Bank forecasting, in its quarterly inflation report, that underlying inflation would be running close to 3.00 percent and rising in two years' time.
"The picture has been complicated by the appreciation of sterling," the Bank said in its report.

"In the short run, the rise in sterling will lead to a fall in inflation as import prices fall. But that is primarily a one-off impact on the domestic price level, rather than a continuing reduction in the underlying rate of inflation."
The Bank said the pound's effective exchange rate had appreciated by 16 percent since August last year.
The government has a medium-term target of 2.5 percent for underlying inflation -- a target Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke expects to be met.

"In the near term, the rise in the exchange rate leads to a fall in the central projection (for inflation). But monetary policy must look beyond the short-term effects and ensure that underlying inflation is consistent with the target," the report said.
Mervin King, the Bank's chief economist, said the inflation forecast had been cut quite significantly in the short term to reflect "this one-off effect".
"That effect lingers for about 12 months or so," he said. Thereafter, inflation is forecast to rise.
The Bank conceded that the pound's rocket-fuelled rally may create an imbalance between exporting firms and those geared to the domestic sector.
Clarke has long maintained that the weakness of UK manufacturing, and exporters in particular, suggested interest rates should not yet rise from their present 6.00 percent.
The Bank also said the pound's strength would lead to a deterioration in Britain's trade performance in volume terms.

"The reduction in the contribution of net trade to output growth does reduce the impact of the strength of domestic demand," it said. "To that extent, it does reduce inflationary pressure over the horizon of the forecast."
But the Bank still maintained that buoyant domestic demand would eventually put upward pressure on inflation. It called for a moderate tightening of policy.

The pound has benefited from expectations of higher UK interest rates than in Europe -- a view that has been exacerbated by falling fiscal deficits in Europe as governments struggle to meet the Maastricht criteria.
A rise in oil prices had bosted oil-rich economies, and the UK in particular, the Bank said in its report.
A shift in demand for UK tradeable goods and services could also have buoyed the pound, it said.
"It is, however, assumed that a small part of the appreciation is purely erratic and likely to be reversed more quickly than current interest rate differentials would imply," the Bank said.
But there is uncertainty about the pound's future path.
"We can't know for certain that those factors account for all the rise in sterling," King said. "There is a good deal of uncertainty ... for that reason."
-- Mike Peacock, London Newsroom +44 171 542 5109
